Do you often fall when walking?

Do you have pain in your hips, knees, or feet when walking?
Have you ever had a stroke or other brain injury?
Have you ever been diagnosed with cerebral palsy?
Do you use the wheelchair behind you because you cannot walk long distances?
Do you feel unsteady or as though you might lose your balance when walking?
Do you experience dizziness or a spinning sensation?
Do you have numbness or reduced sensation in your feet?
Do you have tremors or involuntary movements?
Did this walking difficulty begin suddenly?

Do you currently feel confused or have difficulty concentrating?
Are you slurring your speech?
Do you have difficulty standing with your feet together and your eyes closed?
Have you had vomiting or loss of consciousness?
Have you taken more than the prescribed dose of the sedating medication?
Do you feel that your symptoms are improving as the alcohol or medication wears off?

Do you have a severe headache?
Do you have new weakness, facial drooping, or numbness on one side?
Do you have difficulty swallowing?
Do you have trouble breathing?
Does your walking become noticeably better when you are distracted or not being observed?
Have you had similar episodes of sudden walking difficulty that later resolved?
Did the symptoms begin during or shortly after a major emotional stressor or frightening event?
Have doctors previously found no neurological or physical explanation for these symptoms?
Can you walk normally when urgently trying to avoid danger or reach something?
Did the ataxia begin gradually and progress over months or years rather than truly appearing suddenly?
Have any biological relatives had unexplained poor balance, slurred speech, or a diagnosed cerebellar disorder?
Have you had genetic testing for spinocerebellar ataxias, including an RFC1 repeat-expansion test?
Do you have urinary urgency or incontinence, erectile dysfunction, fainting on standing, or other autonomic symptoms?
Do you have chronic cough, difficulty sensing where your feet are, or impaired vestibular function?
Have you had significant long-term alcohol use?
Have you had thyroid disease, vitamin E deficiency, gluten sensitivity/celiac disease, or cancer?
Have blood tests for autoimmune/paraneoplastic cerebellar ataxia, including anti-GAD65 and anti-Yo/ Hu/ Ri antibodies, been positive?
Have you taken phenytoin, carbamazepine, lithium, metronidazole, amiodarone, or other medications known to cause cerebellar toxicity for a prolonged period?
Have you had recurrent severe vomiting, malnutrition, bariatric surgery, or prolonged nutritional deficiency?
Have you had a preceding viral infection, encephalitis, or other serious infection before the ataxia began?
Have you had repeated episodes of acute worsening of ataxia triggered by fever, exercise, fasting, or emotional stress?
Did the first symptoms actually begin in childhood or adolescence, despite becoming noticeable only recently?
Have you ever had seizures, migraine with neurological symptoms, hearing loss, retinal disease, or muscle weakness?
Have you been exposed chronically to solvents, heavy metals, or recreational drugs?
Has formal neuropsychological testing shown cognitive decline?
Have your balance, gait, or speech progressively worsened over the same five-year period in which cerebellar atrophy progressed on MRI?
Did the ataxia begin after age 25?
Have you developed stiffness, slowness, abnormal eye movements, or limb jerks?
Have repeated examinations shown a purely cerebellar syndrome without sensory loss, pyramidal signs, parkinsonism, or cognitive impairment?
orders: Perform a focused neurological examination including cranial nerves, dysarthria assessment, limb coordination (finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin), gait, tandem gait, and Romberg testing.
Measure bedside capillary blood glucose and vital signs, including oxygen saturation.
Obtain urgent non-contrast CT head with CT angiography of the head and neck.
Obtain an urgent brain MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging if the CT/CTA is nondiagnostic.
Perform urine toxicology screening and a serum ethanol level.

Order comprehensive genetic testing for hereditary cerebellar ataxia, including repeat-expansion analysis for RFC1, FXN, SCA1/2/3/6/7, and FGF14 GAA expansion, plus sequencing/deletion analysis of SPG7, PMPCA, PNKD, SETX, and other recessive ataxia genes.
Test serum vitamin E, vitamin B12, copper, ceruloplasmin, TSH/free T4, folate, lactate, and serum amino acids.
Test tissue-transglutaminase IgA with total IgA, anti-GAD65, and a comprehensive paraneoplastic/autoimmune cerebellar ataxia antibody panel.
Perform lumbar puncture for CSF cell count, protein, glucose, oligoclonal bands, IgG index, and autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody testing.
served: CSF oligoclonal bands and IgG index
